facts: Joshua Foer attended the 2005 U.S. Memory Championship as a journalist.
There he met Ed Cooke, a 24-year-old English memory grandmaster.
After the contest, hours of talk and several rounds of beer at a local bar, Cooke offered to coach him.
Reviews say Foer's own memory was ordinary and that the book's thesis is that memory is a trainable skill.
After about a year of training he won the 2006 USA Memory Championship.
He set a U.S. record in speed cards: one deck in 1 minute 40 seconds.
At the World Memory Championships in London he placed 13th overall and won bronze in names and faces.
The book examines Daniel Tammet, a self-described savant, and Foer comes to suspect he has more in common with the memory-contest competitors than with the Rain Man type of savant.
The book was published in 2011; it debuted at number 3 on the New York Times bestseller list and stayed eight weeks (Wikipedia).

tension: A journalist who came to watch the memory contest ends up winning it a year later; how much of that is training?
opening_idea: Open on the 1:40 deck of cards and the fact that the man who did it had come as a spectator.

lessons.idea: Before writing a skill off as not for you, put a coach and a year of practice next to it.
lessons.anchor: Foer arrives as a reporter and wins after a year with Cooke.
lessons.example: Someone who says she is hopeless with names has never practised with a method.

reflect_final: Which skill have you written off as not for you without ever practising it with someone who already knows the method?

use_cases.situation: A colleague says they are just bad at remembering names.
use_cases.move: Mention that Foer, a journalist with an ordinary memory, trained a year with a coach, and ask if they want to try a method together.

use_cases.situation: You tell yourself you have a bad memory.
use_cases.move: Pick one thing you keep forgetting and ask someone who is good at it how they learned it.

use_cases.situation: A student at home says they cannot memorize.
use_cases.move: Ask them to teach you the method they use and compare it with one from a friend.

pocket_idea: A reporter with an ordinary memory won a national title after a year with a coach, so ask who could teach you.
